Brazilian officials raised concerns with Apple nearly three months ago about minors being able to access gambling apps, and the iPhone maker has now been given five business days to provide further information on its App Store safety measures. Here's what's known so far.

Apple faces regulatory and age verification pressure

Back in April, Brazilian officials wrote separately to Apple and Google, questioning the lack of age restrictions on gambling apps in their app stores.

At the time, the National Secretariat for Digital Rights (Sedigi) and the National Consumer Secretariat (Senacon) each sent letters to the two companies, asking whether there were a "significant number" of apps on their platforms that offered or facilitated minors' access to gambling platforms.

Brazil recently passed new legislation called "ECA Digital," which requires app stores to restrict minors from accessing gambling content — Apple subsequently rolled out age verification for apps rated 18+ in the country.

However, officials said their preliminary investigation found that many gambling apps appear to lack proper age restrictions or federal authorisation, casting doubt on the effectiveness of those safeguards.

Although Apple's full response has not been made public, authorities now say the company has answered most of the initial questions, but additional information is still required.

Below is a statement from Brazil's Ministry of Justice and Public Security (published via Canaltech):

Items still to be clarified include: how regulatory authorisation for apps offered in Brazil is verified; the technical criteria used to distinguish simulation apps from those involving real-money gambling — including cases where approved functionality is later hidden or altered; and existing mechanisms to prevent minors from accessing inappropriate content. Authorities have also requested information on proactive monitoring procedures, risk prioritisation criteria, average takedown time after detection, and a timeline for implementing and announcing remedial measures (including

The secretariat said Google's response was weaker, and has asked the search giant to further explain: how it verifies the identity of authorised operators, how it monitors apps whose licences have been suspended or expired, how it measures enforcement effectiveness, and how it prevents minors from searching for or downloading gambling apps.

Finally, the secretariat demanded that responses from both Apple and Google be made public, while allowing confidential information to be submitted separately under restricted arrangements.
